summary: Deep technical session focusing on how Redwood's async scheduler influences kernel selection heuristics, the tradeoffs between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM execution paths, and how CUDA graph replay/fallback behavior interacts with KV cache usage and VPC/on-prem constraints.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-03
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Rodriguez (Helios, Lead ML Eng), Owen Lee (Helios, Infra), Priya Nair (Helios, Security), Alan Wu (Helios, CTO)

Summary:
- High-level: Evaluate how Redwood's async scheduling layer changes which kernel paths are chosen at runtime, and the downstream effects on latency P95, throughput, and stable CUDA-graph replay.
- Main asks from Helios: determinism for audit logs, predictable tail latency under mixed seq-len loads, and on-prem VPC network patterns for KV cache sync.

Topics discussed:
1) Async scheduler heuristics and how it batches/defers work in presence of priority lanes.
2) Kernel selector: when it picks TensorRT-LLM optimized kernels vs vLLM-style aten paths.
3) CUDA graph recording/replay instability when small batches and dynamic seq-lengths cause kernel mismatch.
4) KV cache affinity and eviction interplay with NVLINK / NUMA on their on-prem nodes.
5) Security: KMS integration and SSO for private deploy.

Action items (quick list in call):
- Redwood to share raw nvprof & nvtx traces and kernel timeline PDF.
- Helios to send request distribution for 30-day window.
- Setup dedicated pilot and on-prem POC date.

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect):
[00:00:00] Sofia Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining we wanted to deep dive on the async scheduler impacts, um, so quick intros and then we'll jump into some traces.
[00:00:10] Maya Rodriguez: hey, maya here, thanks, uh, we're most worried about tail latency when we get bursty web traffic at close of markets so, like, 512 tokens tails.
[00:00:18] Owen Lee: owen infra, we run a mixed cluster, nvlink between some boxes, and we've seen eviction thrash when the KV cache is large.
[00:00:25] Liam Chen: cool, we'll show some cases where the scheduler defers low-priority streams to fill a CUDA graph which can flip kernel choices mid-stream.
[00:00:35] Alan Wu: can you expand on "flip kernel choices"? i thought kernel selection is deterministic per model.
[00:00:40] Liam Chen: right so deterministic at compile time, but at runtime the heuristic picks an optimized path based on batch/seq distribution and whether persistent KV cache is active. with async scheduling, you may aggregate different sequences into the same launch which triggers a different kernel (e.g., tensorrt-llm fused attention vs aten/unfused path)
[00:00:55] Maya Rodriguez: so that means our short requests could end up on a heavier kernel because they got batched with a long request?
[00:00:59] Liam Chen: exactly, and if that happens during CUDA-graph replay the replayed graph might assume a different kernel shape, causing a fallback to a non-graph path or an expensive re-record.
[00:01:12] Priya Nair: that fallback is a compliance concern, we need consistent behavior for reproducible logs for audits.
[00:01:18] Sofia Patel: thanks, noted, we'll show how we can constrain the scheduler to keep lane affinity and force per-lane kernel paths.

[00:02:05] Liam Chen: sharing my screen — okay first trace is a 2-hour sample during a market close spike. you can see at 00:22 we go from 85% trt-llm path to mixed; there's a cluster of 1.7ms tails then jumps to 18ms. nvtx shows graph replay at the same time.
[00:02:30] Maya Rodriguez: can you explain why the TPU... sorry, the "trt" graph would increase latency so much?
[00:02:35] Liam Chen: mmh, it's the shape mismatch — trt kernels are heavily optimized for fixed shapes and fused attention; when the graph is recorded with certain seq-len and then a different session with hybrid seqs hits the replay, the runtime either re-records or falls back to an interpreter path which is slower. plus there is cache pressure on the KV pages so memory copies add overhead.

[00:03:20] Owen Lee: we saw similar when we tried vLLM's continuous batching. is vLLM safer in this case?
[00:03:25] Liam Chen: vLLM's aten path has more dynamic kernels so it's more tolerant to seq-len variance — less re-recording — but for long sequences its per-token cost is higher vs a well-shaped trt kernel. so it's a tradeoff: stability vs peak efficiency.
[00:03:40] Sofia Patel: and our async scheduler introduces one more axis: latency SLOs per lane. if you want deterministic lanes we can pin short requests to a low-latency lane that uses vLLM path and long requests to a throughput lane with trt.

[00:04:12] Alan Wu: how does batching policy interact with CUDA graph recording? can you force no-graph for certain lanes?
[00:04:18] Liam Chen: yes you can opt-out of graph capture per deployment or per lane; we also can set a min batch size and max queue delay which reduces shape churn. one nuance: no-graph increases CPU overhead due to per-launch overhead, so tail might be better but throughput suffers.

[00:05:05] Maya Rodriguez: in our environment we have NUMA boundaries and uneven NVLINK, could that exacerbate KV cache evictions?
[00:05:12] Liam Chen: definitely. eviction patterns look worse if the cache pages aren't pinned to the GPU that runs the kernel. we saw cases where the scheduler moved a request to a different GPU because of load, triggering KV transfer over p2p which spiked latency.
[00:05:30] Owen Lee: is there a way to bind KV cache to a device and also keep the scheduler aware?
[00:05:35] Liam Chen: yep — affinity rules: pin cache to device and configure scheduler to prefer placement. Redwood supports device-affinity hints and a hard affinity mode where requests are routed to the device owning their KV entries. downside is underutilization if skewed.

[00:06:10] Priya Nair: security question: does persistent KV cache touch disk in private deploys? we need to know encryption at rest and KMS key rotation.
[00:06:18] Sofia Patel: for private on-prem, KV entries can be in-enclave or encrypted with your KMS. we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key ops and support key rotation. we can provide SOC2 artifacts for that flow.

[00:07:00] Liam Chen: jumping back to kernel heuristics — here's an example where async scheduling delays small requests by 6ms to coalesce into a larger graph. that small delay allowed a trt-llm fused kernel to be chosen which improved throughput but worsened P99 for those user-facing short queries.
[00:07:15] Maya Rodriguez: so for our SLAs we probably want to avoid coalescing short queries — maybe give them a strict SLA lane?
[00:07:21] Liam Chen: agreed. we also offer adaptive thresholds: below X tokens always go to low-latency lane; between X and Y use mixed heuristics; above Y go throughput-trt.

[00:08:10] Alan Wu: curious about the reproducibility of metrics — when kernel choices flip, our perf dashboards show noise. can we get deterministic kernel assignment for specific model versions?
[00:08:20] Liam Chen: yes there's a pinning config: pin model-version to a path (force vLLM or force TRT). you lose some runtime adaptation but you gain deterministic metrics which helps auditing.

[00:09:05] Maya Rodriguez: about CUDA graphs, we saw a failure where replay threw an error and the request was retried leading to duplicate billing. any ideas?
[00:09:12] Liam Chen: we instrument retries — that scenario usually happens when a recorded graph expects certain scratch sizes; on mismatch the runtime throws and we fallback to interpreter path but sometimes retry logic is aggressive. we can throttle retries and log unique ids so billing systems can dedupe.

[00:10:00] Owen Lee: is there a way to selectively disable graph replay but keep graph capture?
[00:10:05] Liam Chen: you can record graphs for profiling but disable automatic replay in production; then an operator approves a stable graph. it's a safe model for on-prem where determinism matters.

[00:11:00] Sofia Patel: i want to flag a configuration we often recommend for mixed traffic: enable per-lane graph capture but use small per-lane max batch and a 4ms max queue delay. that reduces shape churn while keeping benefits of graph when shapes stabilize.

[00:12:20] Maya Rodriguez: can you share examples of where forcing trt ended up worse than vLLM?
[00:12:27] Liam Chen: sure, we had a customer with a heavy tail of short queries; they forced trt and saw P95 regress because many short queries triggered re-records. switching to vLLM for short lane cut tails by 60% at a cost of ~12% throughput drop overall.

[00:13:40] Alan Wu: any hardware signals we should monitor to detect impending eviction thrash?
[00:13:46] Liam Chen: watch page faults, p2p transfer counters, and per-GPU memory fragmentation metrics; also track KV cache hit ratio and the number of times a request had to wait for cache population. we can add those to the Redwood console as custom charts.

[00:15:00] Maya Rodriguez: on the networking side, our VPC has strict egress controls. how do Redwood private connectors work with peered networks?
[00:15:07] Sofia Patel: Redwood private supports VPC peering and customer-managed NAT; for on-prem we ship an optional connector that initiates an outbound tunnel to the control plane for updates — all traffic can be restricted, and logs go to your logging backend. we can walk through the network diagram offline.

[00:16:05] Owen Lee: i need concrete suggestions: what config should we start the pilot with?
[00:16:10] Liam Chen: propose: two lanes — low-latency pinned to vLLM path (min batch 1, max queue delay 3ms), throughput lane pinned to TRT-LLM path (min batch 8, max queue delay 20ms). enable device affinity for KV and disable auto-replay for graphs; collect nvtx/nvprof traces for first 48 hours.
[00:16:28] Maya Rodriguez: sounds good. can you also limit retry attempts on graph failures? we had billing dupes.
[00:16:33] Liam Chen: yes reduce retries to 1 and enable dedupe ids on requests.

[00:17:20] Sofia Patel: quick question to Priya on security acceptance criteria — will SOC2 + KMS integration + audit logs be sufficient for you to sign?
[00:17:28] Priya Nair: yes that plus a runbook showing how we can rotate keys and confirm no KV data leaves the VPC. we also want SSO via SAML and RBAC enforcement on the console.
[00:17:40] Sofia Patel: we'll include SSO docs and a runbook in the next bundle.

[00:18:50] Liam Chen: sharing a second trace where we intentionally forced mixed batch shapes: see how the runtime re-records graphs at high frequency — that produced CPU stalls at 00:12 and 00:19. the fix was to increase the min stable shape threshold and enable shape bucketing.
[00:19:10] Maya Rodriguez: shape bucketing? explain please.
[00:19:14] Liam Chen: it's grouping sequences into buckets by length (e.g., 8-32, 33-128, 129-512) and only allowing a graph per bucket when a stable pattern emerges. reduces re-records but you need enough traffic per bucket.

[00:20:05] Alan Wu: what about quantization? does int8 or 4-bit change these dynamics?
[00:20:12] Liam Chen: yes, quantization can change kernel availability; certain fused TRT kernels only exist for fp16 or some int8 profiles. with 4-bit you might fall back to aten/unfused paths more often. but for many long-sequence workloads int8 gives huge throughput gains. we recommend profiling quantized kernels early.

[00:21:00] Maya Rodriguez: can Redwood suggest quant profiles per lane?
[00:21:05] Liam Chen: yes Redwood Optimize will suggest quant and kernel profiles per workload; we'll run a recommended profile on pilot cluster and share the delta.

[00:22:10] Owen Lee: any gotchas for on-prem GPUs with older drivers? we manage a few nodes with 470.x driver.
[00:22:16] Liam Chen: older drivers can break certain graph replay features; we recommend tested CUDA + driver matrix (we'll share) and ideally the latest stable runtime used in Redwood images. older drivers may force aten fallback more frequently.

[00:23:40] Sofia Patel: i want to summarize the pilot config again — two lanes, pinned paths, device affinity, graph replay disabled for production, graph capture enabled for profiling, reduce retries, collect nvprof. anyone disagrees?
[00:23:52] Maya Rodriguez: agree.
[00:23:54] Alan Wu: agree.

[00:24:30] Liam Chen: quick note on observability — we'll instrument graph captures, kernel selections and KV cache hits as metadata on each request so you can slice by model/version/lane and produce deterministic SLAs.

[00:25:20] Priya Nair: for auditability we need immutable logs — can the console export immutable events to our SIEM?
[00:25:25] Sofia Patel: yes we support log shipping to customer SIEMs and can set retention policies per customer.

[00:26:40] Maya Rodriguez: about cost — forcing vLLM for short lanes reduces costs or increases?
[00:26:46] Liam Chen: forcing vLLM for short lanes increases per-token cost vs perfectly batched TRT but reduces tail latency. cost depends on request mix; Redwood Optimize will estimate per-lane unit economics.

[00:27:55] Alan Wu: any suggestions for defensive retries to avoid duplicate charges when graph replay fails?
[00:28:00] Liam Chen: use idempotency keys, set retry backoff, and server-side dedupe window for a few seconds. we can set billing to only count completed tokens and ignore dropped duplicates.

[00:29:40] Maya Rodriguez: for the on-prem POC, we'll need a secure install and a verification checklist; can Redwood provide an install playbook?
[00:29:46] Sofia Patel: yes we'll provide an install playbook, checklist, and a runbook for key rotation and SSO.

[00:30:55] Liam Chen: switching topics: kernel mapper heuristics — we use a cost model that accounts for seq-len distribution, batch size, memory pressure, and quant profile. async scheduling changes the observed batch size distribution so we update the cost model online with telemetry.
[00:31:12] Maya Rodriguez: how quickly does that adapt? we worried about oscillation if it flips too fast.
[00:31:16] Liam Chen: we have smoothing windows and hysteresis. the default is a 5-minute smoothing but for enterprise you can set longer windows to avoid oscillations.

[00:32:05] Owen Lee: can we lock hysteresis to avoid kernel flips during critical windows like market close?
[00:32:09] Liam Chen: yes, schedule-based policies: you can set blackout windows where heuristics are locked or use manual pinning.

[00:33:20] Alan Wu: do you support hybrid models where some layers are run in TRT and others in aten?
[00:33:24] Liam Chen: partial fusion is supported in some pipelines; TRT plugins can cover specific attention blocks while fallback for other ops remains in aten. it complicates graph consistency but can be a good compromise.

[00:34:10] Maya Rodriguez: if we do mixed-mode, does KV cache layout change?
[00:34:14] Liam Chen: it can — be careful about where KV is stored and accessed; mixed-mode often requires ensuring pointers and offsets are consistent across kernels. Redwood's runtime can normalize a KV layout to be shared.

[00:35:05] Sofia Patel: quick check — any blockers to starting the pilot next week?
[00:35:09] Owen Lee: we need the network diagram and the pilot sizing doc.
[00:35:12] Maya Rodriguez: and we'll prepare request traces.

[00:36:00] Liam Chen: action item recap: i'll run a stress job with variable batch shapes, capture nvprof/nvtx, and share the traces. sofia will send security pack. helio's team sends traces and VPC diagram.

[00:37:45] Priya Nair: one more security note: we'll run a threat model during POC; expect a few questions about outbound control plane connections.
[00:37:52] Sofia Patel: understood, we'll include network flow specifics and an option for fully private air-gapped deployment if needed.

[00:39:10] Maya Rodriguez: if during the pilot we see persistent spikes, what's the escalation path?
[00:39:15] Sofia Patel: dedicated support channel, SE on-call, and we can open an incident and snapshot kernels for offline analysis.

[00:40:02] Liam Chen: last technical note — for quantized kernels, also watch alignment/padding; some TRT int8 kernels assume 8-aligned tensors so odd sequence lengths cause extra copy overhead. align sequences or use bucket padding.

[00:41:30] Alan Wu: ok that was helpful. can we get a concise playbook doc which lists recommended configs and why?
[00:41:36] Sofia Patel: yes we'll produce a "pilot playbook" with configs, metrics to watch, and an escalations list.

[00:42:50] Maya Rodriguez: question — competitors: we tested Vertex AI endpoints; they didn't expose kernel metrics. Do you?
[00:42:58] Liam Chen: we expose kernel selection, graph captures, and KV metrics as first-class telemetry. you can drill into per-request kernel choices.

[00:44:05] Owen Lee: final quick ask: can Redwood annotate requests with the chosen kernel id so our billing and tracing align?
[00:44:11] Liam Chen: yes we can add kernel_id as metadata; we'll include it in the pilot traces.

[00:45:30] Sofia Patel: wrapping up — next steps again: share nvprof traces (Redwood), request traces and VPC diagram (Helios), schedule on-prem POC (mutual). we'll aim to start pilot the week of 2026-08-10.
[00:45:45] Maya Rodriguez: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[00:45:50] Alan Wu: thanks.
[00:45:55] (end of recording)

Notes about transcription quality: some technical terms may be mis-heard (e.g., "TRT LLM" shown as "trt-llm", "nvtx" occasionally transcribed as "nv t x"), and a few timestamps approximate the spoken times.
